what: Expanding cage of angulated scissors (the Hoberman principle). Three mutually perpendicular rings of eight scissor cells each, 48 rigid kinked links in all, are coupled so that they open together. Each link has two 48 mm arms meeting at a fixed 135° kink. Motor A drives the cage through two 8:24 gear pairs and a worm on an 8-tooth gear, a 72:1 reduction. The program opens the cage from scissor angle θ = 48° to 30° (1296 motor degrees), checks the actual size, holds for a second and closes it again. Here θ is the angle between an arm and the ring’s tangent at its inner pivot.
try: Open Bloom with its program, press Reset, then Run. The program first measures three inner spans, the distance between opposite inner pivots in each ring, and refuses to start unless each is about 8.4 cm.

Stage 2 turns motor A 1296° at 144°/s (about 9 s). The scissor angle changes by only 18°, but watch the inner opening of each ring: it should grow from about 8.4 cm to about 15.3 cm across, while the outermost pivots move out only from about 22.6 cm to 24.9 cm.
Follow one ring: every pivot moves along a straight line through the centre, and each cell keeps covering exactly 45° of the circle. The ring changes size, not shape.

After each move the program corrects the motor using the measured spans, at most three small trims, because it trusts the actual cage rather than the motor angle. Stage 3 holds, stage 4 closes the cage and trims back to the starting span.
why: Each kinked link has two arms of length a = 48 mm at a fixed angle of 135° = 180° − 360°/8. With exactly this kink a ring of eight cells closes for every scissor angle, and all pivots slide along fixed radial lines: the inner pivots sit at radius r = a·cos(θ + 22.5°)/sin 22.5°, the outer ones at R = a·cos(θ − 22.5°)/sin 22.5°. With straight scissor rods the angle covered by each cell would change and the ring could not close at every size; the kink keeps each cell at 45°. From θ = 48° to 30°, r grows from about 42 mm to 76 mm (×1.82) but R only from 113 mm to 124 mm (×1.10): the inner opening blooms much more than the outside grows.
matters: Deployable structures such as expanding domes, retractable roofs, folding antennas and the Hoberman sphere toy use angulated scissors, because one input changes the size of the whole structure while it keeps its shape. The 72:1 drive trades speed for force: 1296 motor degrees change θ by just 18°. The program trims the motor from measured spans instead of trusting the motor angle; in the simulator the cage settled about 0.3 cm small before the first trim and closed with about 23 motor degrees of slack. In two headless runs of the Brickwright simulator the cage opened and closed without failing: each of the 48 links turned 18.06° ± 0.09° for 1296 motor degrees (18.00° predicted), and the reported inner span reached 15.2–15.3 cm (15.27 cm predicted). That is a simulation observation; no physical LEGO build has been tested.
question: The program changes θ from 48° to 30°. Do the inner opening and the outside size of a ring grow by the same factor?
answer: No. The inner radius r = a·cos(θ + 22.5°)/sin 22.5° grows from about 41.9 mm to 76.4 mm, a factor of about 1.82. The outer radius R = a·cos(θ − 22.5°)/sin 22.5° grows only from about 113.2 mm to 124.4 mm, a factor of about 1.10. Their difference, the ring’s radial depth R − r = 2a·sin θ, shrinks from about 71 mm to 48 mm as the cage opens.
further: Check the program’s trim factors against the geometry: dr/dθ = −a·sin(θ + 22.5°)/sin 22.5°. Through 72:1 this gives about 0.0057 cm of inner span per motor degree at θ = 48° and 0.0048 cm at 30° – the trimScale values in the program.
Calculate where the inner pivots would meet in the centre (r = 0 at θ = 67.5°), then look at the model for what would collide long before that.
Bloom is three great-circle rings, not a complete Hoberman sphere. Count which pivots are shared where two rings cross and why that forces all three rings to open together.

Limits: the part position reporters round to 1 mm, and three spans are only a coarse check of a 781-part model. Rigid links and ideal pins are assumed; a real cage would sag under its weight and wobble in its pin clearances.
formula: a = 48 mm (120 LDU), n = 8 cells, kink = 180° − 360°/n = 135°. Inner radius r = a·cos(θ + 180°/n)/sin(180°/n); outer radius R = a·cos(θ − 180°/n)/sin(180°/n); R − r = 2a·sin θ. θ = 48° → inner span 2r ≈ 8.37 cm; θ = 30° → 2r ≈ 15.27 cm. Drive 72:1: |Δθ| = Δmotor/72, so 1296° → 18°.
